catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cowl:
This liturgical entry traces the cowl, the hood worn in many religious orders, from a grocer's bag to a ceremonial garment. The name first meant a sack for wares, then a shaped article of dress like it. Outdoor cloaks of the ancient world often carried a hood at the back, to pull up over the head.

Monks adopted the hood early: Sozomen, Jerome, and Cassian all mention it, and St. Benedict ordered warm and light cowls for winter and summer. Over time the cowl grew into a great cloak with a hood for choir use among Benedictines and Cistercians. Franciscans wear a smaller hood fixed to the habit, while bishops and cardinals wear one on the cappa. Colours follow the habit.

the-brass-bowl:
Louis Joseph Vance wrote The Brass Bowl, dated 1907. The first part is called Dust. In the dull hot dusk of a summer day a green touring car swings out of the East Drive. It pulls up sharp at the Fifty-ninth Street tracks, then crosses the Plaza under the calm eye of a mounted traffic man. South on the Avenue it joins the press of cars.

Four young men ride in the back, all more or less hid in dust, dusters, and goggles. In truth he is set apart. He is Daniel Maitland, a man of means and rank in the social and cash worlds. His whole-hearted part in wild pranks has won him the love of the young set and the name Mad Maitland. Yet now he looks bored with the mad drive his own rash words set off.
the-tale-of-solomon-owl: Arthur Scott Bailey published Solomon Owl with Grosset and Dunlap in 1917, with illustrations by Harry L. Smith. The record at hand gives the title page, contents, and picture list, but no chapter text, so Solomon's night rounds stay hidden. Twenty-two chapters promise scares for Johnny Green, a taste for frogs, an odd bargain, a Hallowe'en episode, and Solomon hanging by his heels. Cousin Simon Screecher arrives later for a cousinly quarrel. Even in outline, Solomon comes across as a proud night hunter among Bailey's farm and woodland creatures.
the-wolf-s-long-howl:
Stanley Waterloo's The Wolf's Long Howl, published in 1899, collects twenty-one short stories. Titles range from An Ulm to Christmas 200,000 B.C. Several stories turn on love, crime, and forest tragedy. The title story opens with George Henry Harrison. He is thirty, well connected, and used to hearty company.

Harrison had never thought himself alone in the world. Waterloo notes his social standing and quick mind. Yet happiness has begun to slip from him. That quiet unease launches the tale. Readers who like varied short fiction will find romances, mysteries, and tall tales side by side in one volume.
